value.overview: The Green Ibis (Mesembrinibis cayennensis), also called the Cayenne Ibis, is a dark, forest-associated wading bird of the ibis family. Its plumage can show green, bronze, and blue iridescence in good light, although birds in shaded habitats often appear nearly black. Unlike many ibises, it is usually secretive and is most often encountered alone or in pairs along quiet streams, forest swamps, muddy paths, and wet lowland woodland.
value.classification: The Green Ibis belongs to the ibis and spoonbill family Threskiornithidae and is the only living species in the genus Mesembrinibis. It is classified in the order Pelecaniformes.
value.identification: This medium-sized ibis has an overall dark greenish-black appearance with subtle metallic green or bronze reflections, especially on the neck, breast, and upperparts. It has a long, slender, downcurved bill that is greenish with a paler or yellowish tip, and relatively short, dull green legs. The body looks compact and heavy compared with the more slender Glossy Ibis. In Costa Rica, its quiet, forested wetland habitat and dark plumage help distinguish it from more open-country ibises.
value.rangeHabitat: The Green Ibis ranges from eastern Honduras and Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama, then across much of tropical South America to northern Argentina and Paraguay. It uses swampy forest, wooded marshes, flooded woodland, forested river margins, gallery forest, muddy pools, and occasionally mangrove-edge wetlands, mainly in the lowlands. In Costa Rica it is a resident but localized species, occurring chiefly in Caribbean-slope lowlands, including the Río Frío area and coastal wetlands north and south of Limón. It may also occur locally in suitable forested wetlands around Sarapiquí.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally resident in Costa Rica and across most of its range. Regular long-distance migration is not known, although birds may make short local or seasonal movements, particularly as water levels and feeding conditions change.
value.breeding: The Green Ibis breeds in wooded wetlands and along forested waterways, where it places its nest in vegetation, usually above or near water. Available observations indicate that nesting activity can occur in Costa Rica, including the Sarapiquí region. The nest is a platform made from sticks and other plant material. Detailed information on clutch size, incubation, and parental care is limited for this secretive species, and breeding timing may vary with local rainfall and flooding patterns.
value.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly in shallow water, wet mud, leaf litter, and saturated ground. The curved bill is used to probe and sweep through soft substrate for invertebrates such as insects, worms, and snails. It may also take small aquatic animals, including amphibians or fish, as well as some plant material. Feeding usually takes place along quiet forest streams, marsh edges, muddy trails, and openings beside wooded wetlands.
value.behavior: Green Ibises are generally shy and less social than many other ibises. They are most often seen singly or in pairs, though small groups may gather where food is concentrated. They frequently remain under forest cover and can be difficult to detect until they move into a muddy opening or wetland margin. Activity is often greatest around dawn and dusk, when their rolling calls may reveal their presence. Their flight is strong but somewhat heavy, with the neck extended.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to be undergoing a sufficiently rapid decline to qualify for a threatened category. Precise population estimates and detailed national trend information are limited, especially for localized populations in Central America.
